title: The sandals and the promise
hookLine: two brothers argue on a mountain, each trying to give the other a kingdom
carry: satya: rama keeps even his father's word

lines: A FIGHT TO GIVE THINGS AWAY.
cards: On Chitrakoot, two brothers have an inheritance fight that runs backward: each one is trying to give the kingdom away.

Bharata reaches the hut, sees Rama in bark clothes with matted hair, and falls at his feet, unable to finish a sentence. Rama lifts him up, holds him, and asks the question Bharata has dreaded the whole road.
Where is our father? Why have you left him to come here?

teach.h: WATER FOR A FATHER AT THE MANDAKINI.
teach.b: Bharata tells him. The king is dead, grieving for you. Rama falls like a cut tree.
When he can stand, he goes down to the Mandakini with his brothers and Sita, and offers his father water and a ball of ingudi pulp, the forest food they've been living on.
In Valmiki's telling, he says: what a person eats, their ancestors eat too. Then the arguing begins, and it goes on and on.
Bharata pleads: come home, be king, I'll serve you. Counselors and priests plead. Rama's answer never changes.
Our father gave his word to Kaikeyi and made a promise to me. Keeping his word is how I honor him now. Fourteen years in the forest is my part; ruling Ayodhya is yours.
Bharata even threatens to sit fasting at the door of the hut until Rama gives in, and Rama gently tells him that isn't the way. Finally Bharata asks for one thing.
He brings out a pair of sandals adorned with gold, and asks Rama to step into them, then give them to him. Rama does. Bharata bows to the sandals.
For fourteen years, he says, these will rule. I'll live outside the city in bark and matted hair, waiting for you. And if you're not back the day after fourteen years end, I'll enter the fire.
Notice whose promise Rama is keeping: not his own, his father's, and his father is gone. Hindus call this satya, truth, and keeping your word is one of its plainest forms.

teach.h: SATYA: LET LIFE GO, NEVER THE WORD.
teach.b: In Tulsidas's Hindi Ramayana, Dasharatha names it as the custom of Rama's family, in a line families still quote: let life go, but never the word.

how: Rama's sandals, the padukas, are honored in Hindu worship and art, and Ramlila performances stage the brothers' meeting at Chitrakoot.

o: Rama's bow, which he hands Bharata to guard Ayodhya
Rama's sandals, which Bharata takes home to rule in his name
a gift of gold Bharata brings to win Rama back home

p: the forest food offered to the ancestors

s: Rama agrees to return after Bharata's pleading
he refuses every plea: keeping his father's word comes first.
Rama steps into the sandals before giving them
Bharata asks him to, then bows to them.
Bharata vows to enter fire if Rama is late
if Rama isn't back the day after fourteen years end.

games.q: you're Rama. your brother, the priests, everyone begs you to come home and be king. the father who made the promise is dead. what do you do?
o: go home. the promise died with him.
stay. his word is still his word, and i keep it for him.
games.why: Rama keeps his father's word for him. that's satya, and Bharata answers with the sandals.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open: to a parent, a friend, yourself. Don't judge it. Hold it the way Rama held his father's word, as something alive.
If you pray, offer it quietly to God; if you don't, just say to yourself on each breath out: I'll keep it.

wordCard.voice: The sandals. Rama steps into a pair of gold-adorned sandals and gives them to Bharata, who will set them on the throne for fourteen years.

orig.note: Sanskrit pādukā: a sandal or wooden shoe. Rama's pādukā are still honored in temples and homes.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, Rama keeps even his father's word. Neither brother wins, and neither breaks a promise. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 99–103 (the meeting; the news; the offering at the Mandakini)
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 104–112 (the pleas; Rama's refusal; the sandals)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand (Dasharatha to Kaikeyi on the Raghu family custom: life may go, but not the word)
